restaurants.description:
Led by chef Kwon Woojoong, Kwonsooksoo is a Korean fine-dining restaurant that interprets Korean ingredients and traditional cooking techniques through a contemporary lens. The restaurant makes its own jang and kimchi in-house, with fermentation forming an important foundation of its cuisine. Kwon also focuses on nurturing young chefs as he prepares for “Kwonsooksoo 3.0,” the restaurant’s next chapter in exploring the possibilities of Korean cuisine.

Korean ceramics and crafts are incorporated throughout the dining experience, complementing the food and reflecting the restaurant’s minimalist interpretation of Korean aesthetics.

The main course features a generous spread of traditional Korean dishes, bringing together a diverse range of flavors on one table. Pairings of traditional Korean liquors and wine are also available.

restaurants.name: Leebukbang
restaurants.description:
Drawing on North Korean recipes and food traditions passed down through his family, chef Choi Ji-hyung reinterprets sundae (Korean blood sausage) and other regional dishes with a contemporary approach. Sundae forms the centerpiece of the course, ranging from traditional preparations to creative variations incorporating different ingredients, alongside seasonal dishes inspired by the cuisine of various regions in North Korea. The wood-centered interior, including a bar counter made from beams and doors salvaged from a century-old hanok, provides a fitting backdrop for his cuisine.

restaurants.name: Myeon Seoul
restaurants.description:
Following YUN Seoul, chef Kim Doyun opened myeon-seoul as a more casual restaurant dedicated to his house-made noodles. Made without chemical additives, the noodles combine whole wheat with mung beans and soybeans, using a blend of Korean, French and Turkish wheat to achieve the desired flavor and texture. The menu ranges from fresh perilla oil noodles, which highlight the nutty character of the noodles themselves, to goldongmyeon, alongside dishes such as Seoul Duck, available by advance reservation, and crispy pork belly.
Seoul Duck ₩120,000-
Fresh Perilla Oil Noodles (Vegan) ₩14,000-

Western culinary techniques are combined with distinctly Korean elements such as jang, namul and fermentation, while ingredients and seasonings developed in-house add further depth. Traditional dishes including abalone baechuseon and eomandu are also presented in contemporary forms, shaping a distinctive expression of Korean cuisine.

restaurants.name: Bongraeheon
restaurants.description:
Set within the hanok and gardens of Mayfield Hotel Seoul, Bongraeheon offers a serene setting for traditional Korean royal court cuisine. The hanok was built using traditional techniques by master carpenter Lee Il-gu, who participated in the restoration of Gyeongbokgung Palace. Head chef Lee Geum-hee presents dishes rooted in royal court traditions, including seongnyutang and chilled prawns dressed with Gapyeong pine nut sauce. Gochujang, doenjang and ganjang are made and aged in-house, contributing depth to the clean, balanced flavors of the cuisine.
Lunch Course ₩70,000-

restaurants.name: Sancho
restaurants.description:
Drawing on seasonal ingredients from across the Korean Peninsula, particularly the Taean Peninsula on the west coast, Sancho specializes in regional Korean cuisine. Its signature dishes include ganjang gejang, roe-filled female crabs marinated in house-made soy sauce, and spicy seasoned female crab. The menu also features gegukji, a regional specialty of Chungcheong Province, offering a broader taste of the ingredients and culinary traditions of Korea’s west coast.

restaurants.name: Seoryung
restaurants.description:
After beginning in Hongcheon and later moving to Ganghwa, Seoryung expanded to Seoul. Run by Lee Kyung-hee and Jeong Jong-mun, the restaurant specializes in Pyeongyang-style naengmyeon. At its Cheongdam location, pure buckwheat noodles are served in a variety of ways, from the signature Seoryung Sunmyeon with Hanwoo broth to bibim and perilla oil variations. Dumplings, pork jowl and Hanwoo sirloin bulgogi are also available.
Seoryung Sunmyeon ₩18,000

Seasonal vegetables and other carefully selected ingredients are prepared to preserve their natural flavors, with charcoal adding further depth and texture. Elements drawn from Korean royal cuisine and traditional dining culture are presented in contemporary compositions, while a more concise set menu of Korean dishes is offered at lunch.

Her approach is rooted in memories of the generous meals prepared by her mother, where numerous banchan were each carefully made yet came together in harmony. Drawing freely on ingredients and culinary influences encountered in everyday life, Woo keeps the flavors and sensibilities of Korean cuisine at the core while presenting traditional dishes from her own perspective.

Its distinctive broth is made by simmering hanwoo beef shank and seasoning it simply with salt and soy sauce, producing a pronounced beef flavor and savory depth that complements the buckwheat noodles. Another signature is Seoul-style bulgogi, cooked at the table on a traditional domed grill and often enjoyed alongside the naengmyeon.

restaurants.description:
Pairing traditional Korean liquors with seasonal food, Yuroc brings Korea’s dining and drinking culture into a contemporary bar setting. Its seasonal menu draws on historical dishes such as pogye, based on a recipe from the Sangayorok, and gyuasang, a traditional summer delicacy. A wide selection of Korean liquors, particularly cheongju, complements the food. Meaning the pale green of willow leaves in spring, the name Yuroc evokes both the color of clear cheongju and the leisurely tradition of enjoying a drink.

Pogye ₩22,000-

Inspired by Korea’s 24 seasonal divisions and the changing rhythms of nature, Son combines ingredients at their peak, from shellfish to native varieties of rice, with contemporary culinary techniques. Each dish is accompanied by an illustrated card depicting its key ingredient, offering further insight into the produce and the composition of the dish.

restaurants.name: Haenam Cheonilgwan
restaurants.description:
With roots in Cheonil Sikdang, established in Haenam in 1924, Haenam Cheonilgwan preserves the culinary traditions and family recipes of Korea’s southern Jeolla region under owner Lee Hwa-young. Seasonal ingredients and carefully selected seasonings form the basis of generous table settings featuring specialties such as banji kimchi, chili kimchi with freshwater shrimp jeotgal, and tteokgalbi. By preserving dishes, techniques and ingredients that have become less common over time, the restaurant carries a century of Namdo culinary tradition into the present.

Chachaithe is a tea and confectionery shop in Hannam-dong offering sweets designed to complement both Eastern and Western teas. Using seasonal ingredients, it creates a variety of tea confections inspired by dessert traditions from both cultures. The sweets are also available for purchase as gifts, while its intimate tea room offers a tea and confectionery experience by reservation. The second floor displays a collection of teaware sourced from Korea and abroad.

cafes.name: Crémiel
cafes.description:
Crémiel is a French pâtisserie run by pastry chefs Mickaël Mégnien Boeha and Ji Su-jeong. Its pastries are made with French Label Rouge flour, AOP-certified butter, and antibiotic-free milk and eggs, while all doughs, jams, and creams are prepared in-house. The selection includes classic French pastries such as croissants, pains au chocolat, kouign-amann, and canelés.
Flan Parisien ₩7,000-
Chausson aux Pommes ₩6,500-

cafes.name: Taegeukdang
cafes.description:
Established in 1946, Taegeukdang is the oldest bakery in Seoul. Its name and rose of Sharon emblem reflect the founder’s aspirations for Korea at the beginning of the post-liberation era. The bakery continues to make breads and sweets such as red bean buns and castella using long-standing recipes, while its milk monaka remains a signature enjoyed across generations.

Red Bean Bun ₩3,000-

cafes.name: Pâtisserie MÛR
cafes.description:
Led by chef Choi Kyusung, Pâtisserie MÛR builds on classic French pastry with Korean ingredients and contemporary sensibilities. Its refined creations focus on the character of each ingredient and the flavors developed over time, with baked goods such as brandy cake at the heart of the selection. The pâtisserie aims to make carefully crafted pastry a natural part of everyday life.
Brandy Cake ₩85,000-
Petit Cake ₩12,000

cafes.description:
Passion 5 is SPC Group’s first flagship store and a long-standing dessert destination in Hannam-dong. Divided into bakery, pâtisserie, chocolate, and café sections, it offers a wide selection of cakes, tarts, baked sweets, and pastries. Its extensive range includes elaborate desserts, Baumkuchen, and assorted baked goods for gifts.

cafes.name: Près de Moi Nonhyeon
cafes.description:
Près de Moi is a bakery run by chef Yoon Hwa-young, who has worked in French cuisine for more than 20 years. Baguettes, campagne, focaccia, and loaves are made with French flour and natural sourdough, then used for sandwiches prepared to order. The menu includes sandwiches with house-made terrine, corned beef, and jambon, as well as French dinner dishes.
Reuben Sandwich ₩21,000-
Jambon Cheese or Jambon-Beurre Sandwich ₩18,000-

cafes.name: Fritz Coffee Company, Dohwa
cafes.description:
Founded by a team of coffee professionals, Fritz Coffee Company has focused on making high-quality coffee approachable and accessible. Its carefully sourced and roasted coffees are served alongside bread and pastries from its own bakery, while branding inspired by familiar Korean imagery gives Fritz a distinctive identity. Housed in a renovated old-style Korean residence, the Dohwa location brings its coffee and bakery culture together in one of the brand’s signature spaces.

Long Black ₩5,300-

cafes.description:
House of Shinsegae Dessert Salon presents teas and traditional sweets developed by the Shinsegae Korean Food Research Institute through its study of Korea’s seasons, natural ingredients, and refreshment culture. Each menu uses seasonal Korean produce and traditional preparation methods interpreted in a contemporary format. Its composed setting offers a considered introduction to the flavors and presentation of Korean tea and sweets.

His creations include juak made from glutinous rice dough fermented with makgeolli and yakgwa that is baked rather than fried. Through an ongoing exploration of traditional ingredients and techniques, HAAP offers a modern perspective on Korean rice cakes and confections.

Alongside the brand’s established coffee menu, this location offers exclusive items including lemonade, mousse cakes, and highballs.

The menu includes seasonal items made with Korean ingredients, soft serve made with Sangha Farm milk, and coffee drinks topped with the ice cream.
